title: When Romantic Desire Becomes the Center of Your Entire Future
paragraphs: When Romantic Desire Becomes the Center of Your Entire Future

The relationship you keep asking God to give you may not be the deepest thing your heart is actually asking for—and sometimes the most dangerous idol is not something evil, but something beautiful you have asked to do what only Jesus can do.
There is a version of your future that you may have rehearsed so many times it almost feels like a memory.
Someone finally chooses you.
Not temporarily. Not ambiguously. Not with mixed signals and disappearing messages. They choose you clearly.

There is a wedding. A home. Maybe children. Morning coffee beside someone who stayed. Someone notices when you are quiet. Someone reaches for your hand without being asked. Someone knows the wounds behind your jokes and does not leave when they see them.
And somewhere inside that picture is a sentence you may never say aloud:
Then I will finally be okay.
That sentence is where we need to stop.
Because wanting marriage is not the problem.
Wanting companionship is not the problem.

Wanting to be known, desired, held, pursued, and loved is not automatically sinful. Scripture does not require Christians to become emotionally numb before they become spiritually mature. Marriage is God's creation, not Satan's invention. Scripture can describe the finding of a wife as receiving something good from the Lord (Proverbs 18:22), and the Bible can celebrate marital desire without embarrassment.
So this is not an article telling you to stop wanting love.
It is asking something much more uncomfortable:
What happens when romantic love stops being one beautiful possibility within your future and becomes the thing that gives your entire future permission to matter?
Because you can desire marriage...
and quietly worship what you imagine marriage will give you.
You can pray for a spouse...
and slowly make a spouse your functional savior.
You can say, “God, I trust You,” while internally adding, as long as Your plan eventually includes the person I want.
And that is where a beautiful desire can become a brutal master.
Maybe you know exactly what that feels like.
Another engagement announcement appears on your screen.
You smile.
You tap the heart.
“Congratulations!”
And you mean it.
Mostly.
Then something aches.
You put the phone down, and suddenly your room feels quieter than it did thirty seconds ago.
Another person found someone.
Another wedding.
Another anniversary.
Another pregnancy announcement.
Another smiling photograph beneath words about answered prayers.
And somewhere beneath your genuine happiness for them comes the question you are almost ashamed to ask:
Jesus... what about me?
You have prayed.
You have tried to surrender.
You have deleted the app and downloaded it again.
You have promised yourself you would stop checking their profile.
You have wondered whether you were too picky, not attractive enough, too damaged, too late, too intimidating, too ordinary, too spiritual, not spiritual enough.
Maybe somebody left.
Maybe somebody almost chose you.
Maybe the person you imagined standing beside you in your future is now standing beside somebody else.
That kind of grief is real.
God does not need you to pretend it isn't.
But pain becomes spiritually dangerous when disappointment begins rewriting your theology.
If God loved me, He would give me this.
If I were enough, someone would have chosen me.
If I remain single, my life will somehow be less complete.
Once I find the right person, then my real life can begin.
Read that last sentence again.
Because there is a graveyard filled with years that people accidentally buried beneath the word someday.
Someday, when I'm married.
Someday, when someone chooses me.
Someday, when I have the family.
Someday, when I am finally wanted.
Someday...
I will live.
But Jesus never told you to postpone obedience until romance arrives.
He never said, “Seek first a relationship, and when you finally feel secure enough, pursue My kingdom.”
He said:
ζητεῖτε δὲ πρῶτον τὴν βασιλείαν... καὶ τὴν δικαιοσύνην αὐτοῦ
Zēteite de prōton tēn basileian... kai tēn dikaiosynēn autou.
“Seek first His kingdom and His righteousness...” (Matthew 6:33).
The Greek matters.
ζητεῖτε — zēteite — “seek.”
Not casually notice.
Not occasionally remember.
Seek.
Pursue.
Make this the governing direction of your life.
And then comes the word that exposes us:
πρῶτον — prōton — “first.”
First.

Jesus is talking in context about anxiety over life's necessities, not specifically giving a teaching about dating. We should not rip His words from their setting and pretend Matthew 6:33 is secretly a romance verse. But the kingdom priority He commands reaches straight into this struggle: the Father's kingdom and righteousness belong at the center, while everything else must take its rightful place beneath Him.
Not first until someone attractive notices you.
Not first until you turn thirty.
Not first because God will reward you with a spouse.
First.
Period.
And perhaps that exposes something.
Some of us have turned Christianity into a transaction without realizing it.
God, I stayed pure. Where is my spouse?
God, I prayed. Where is my spouse?
God, I stopped dating the wrong people. Where is my spouse?
God, I served You. Where is my spouse?
As though obedience were currency placed into a heavenly vending machine and marriage were the product we were promised.
But Jesus is not a strategy for getting the life you really want.
Jesus is the treasure.
That changes everything.
Because if Jesus is merely the bridge between you and your dream life, then your dream life—not Jesus—is actually sitting on the throne.
And idols are cruel.
Especially beautiful idols.
An idol does not have to look demonic.
Sometimes an idol wears a wedding dress.
Sometimes it has the face of the person who left you.
Sometimes it is the imaginary husband you have not met.
Sometimes it is the imaginary wife you believe will heal your loneliness.
Sometimes it is the family photograph you desperately want to take five years from now.
The problem is not that those things are ugly.
The problem is that they are not God.
And whatever you ask to carry the weight of God will eventually collapse underneath you.
Marriage cannot bear the weight of your identity.
A husband cannot carry the responsibility of proving your worth.
A wife cannot become your permanent source of peace.
Romance cannot cleanse your guilt.
Sex cannot reconcile you to God.
Being desired cannot erase your sin.
A wedding ring cannot resurrect your soul.
Only Christ can.
And perhaps that is why this hurts so much.
Because sometimes God is not merely confronting what we want.
He is revealing what we expected that desire to save us from.
Maybe you do not simply want marriage.
Maybe you want marriage to prove you are lovable.
Maybe you want someone attractive to choose you because rejection convinced you that your value must be externally verified.
Maybe you want a relationship because silence feels unbearable.
Maybe you want a spouse because you are frightened that nobody will be there when you grow old.
Maybe romance has become your imagined escape from insecurity, sexual temptation, family dysfunction, loneliness, boredom, shame, or the terrifying possibility of being forgotten.
And then Jesus comes near—not to mock the desire, but to ask for the throne beneath it.
This is where surrender becomes painful.
Because surrender does not mean pretending you no longer care.
Surrender sounds more like:
Jesus, I still want this.
I still hope for marriage.
I still feel lonely sometimes.
I still wonder whom I might meet.
I still want to love someone deeply and be loved faithfully.
But You may not have to give me my preferred future in order to remain good.
That sentence can cost tears.
Because surrender is not telling God that your desire is meaningless.
It is telling your desire that God is greater.
Paul speaks into this with words modern Christian culture sometimes struggles to hear.
In 1 Corinthians 7:32, the Greek text begins:
Θέλω δὲ ὑμᾶς ἀμερίμνους εἶναι. ὁ ἄγαμος μεριμνᾷ τὰ τοῦ κυρίου...
Thelō de hymas amerimnous einai. Ho agamos merimna ta tou Kyriou...

Paul's concern is that believers be free from distracting concern, and he describes the unmarried person as able to concern himself with “the things of the Lord”—with how to please the Lord. He later explains that his aim is not to put a restraint upon believers, but to promote devotion to the Lord without distraction.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not describe singleness as God's waiting room.
He does not speak as though unmarried Christians are unfinished humans waiting for their “real” lives to arrive.
And in the same chapter, Paul does not condemn marriage. He explicitly allows and honors marriage while also showing that marriage brings legitimate earthly responsibilities.
That destroys two errors at once.
Marriage is not inferior spirituality.
Singleness is not inferior humanity.
Your marital status is not the measurement of your completeness in Christ.
This matters because Christian culture can accidentally communicate something Scripture does not.
We ask single adults, “So, are you seeing anyone?”
Again.
And again.
And again.
As if this were the primary plotline of their existence.
We celebrate engagements loudly and sometimes barely notice years of quiet faithfulness.
We can make twenty-three-year-olds panic because they have not “found someone.”
We can make thirty-five-year-olds feel as though something went wrong.
We can make divorced people feel permanently branded.
We can make widows and widowers feel as though the greatest chapter of their lives has already closed.
But the Gospel tells a radically different story.
The most complete human being who ever walked this earth was unmarried.
Jesus Christ did not need romantic love to validate His humanity.
He did not need marriage to make His life meaningful.
He did not need another human being to complete Him.
And yet He knew love more deeply than we can comprehend.
He knew friendship.
He knew betrayal.
He knew affection.
He knew grief.
He knew rejection.
He knew what it was to have people leave.
He knew what it was to love people who would fail Him.
Then He went to a cross.
And there, Jesus answered a question deeper than:
Will anybody ever choose me romantically?
He answered:
Can someone like me ever be reconciled to God?
Yes.
But not cheaply.
At Calvary, the sinless Son of God gave Himself for sinners.
Your greatest problem was never singleness.
It was sin.
Your deepest need was never a soulmate.
It was reconciliation with the holy God you had sinned against.
And your greatest rescue is not somebody finally saying, “I choose you.”
It is Christ crucified and risen, calling sinners to repent and believe the Gospel.
That is where romantic idolatry begins losing its grip.
Not when you convince yourself relationships are unnecessary.
But when something infinitely greater fills the center.
Jesus.
Jesus when the messages stop.
Jesus when everybody around you seems to be getting married.
Jesus when someone rejects you.
Jesus when desire burns and obedience hurts.
Jesus when you are forty and the story did not unfold according to the timeline you wrote at twenty-two.
Jesus if marriage comes.
Jesus if marriage does not come soon.
Jesus if your heart gets broken.
Jesus if God rebuilds it.
Jesus in the longing.
Jesus above the longing.
Jesus at the center.
And if God gives you marriage someday, this surrender will not make you love your spouse less.
It may finally teach you how to love them properly.
Because when another human being no longer has to be your god, they are finally free to be human.
They can disappoint you without destroying your identity.
They can have weaknesses without collapsing your universe.
They can fail to read your mind.
They can have difficult days.
They can grow old.
They can need forgiveness.
They can need grace.
And you can love them not as your savior...
but as your neighbor, your covenant companion, and—if both of you belong to Christ—a fellow redeemed sinner walking toward Jesus.
That kind of love is freer.
Healthier.
Holier.
Because two people desperately demanding, Complete me, will eventually exhaust each other.
But two people learning to say, Christ is Lord; let us follow Him together, have discovered a foundation deeper than romance.
So perhaps the question is not merely:
Do you want to get married?
The better question is:
What have you made marriage mean?
Does it mean you finally matter?
Does it mean you finally won?
Does it mean you are finally attractive enough?
Does it mean God finally proved He loves you?
Does it mean your life finally begins?
Does it mean the loneliness finally disappears forever?
If so, do not merely ask God for the relationship.
Ask Him to expose the altar.
Because there may be something underneath your romantic desire that needs to die before it destroys your ability to love.
And that is not cruelty.
That is grace.
Grace sometimes feels like God pulling your fingers away from something you were clutching so tightly that you could no longer receive Him with open hands.
Maybe you have already compromised because romance became too important.
You ignored convictions.
You accepted breadcrumbs.
You stayed in a relationship you knew was dragging you from Christ.
You crossed sexual boundaries and then learned to rename conviction as “being too religious.”
You tolerated manipulation because being mistreated seemed less frightening than being alone.
You kept returning to someone God was using circumstances and wisdom to remove from your life.
You became emotionally dependent on attention.
You flirted because silence made you feel invisible.
You entertained people you knew you should not build a future with because at least somebody wanted you.
Maybe you know exactly where you compromised.
Then hear this carefully:
The Gospel does not say, “You ruined everything.”
The Gospel says there is forgiveness for sinners who come to Christ.
Repentance is not God humiliating you.
Repentance is turning from sin toward the One whose mercy is greater than your scandal.
Peter denied Jesus.
The thief beside Christ had no lifetime left with which to impress God.
The Samaritan woman in John 4 carried a complicated relational history into a conversation with Jesus.
Again and again, Scripture refuses to let human failure write the final sentence when grace enters the story.
That does not make sin harmless.
It makes Christ glorious.
Maybe your romantic history is messy.
Maybe you gave yourself to someone who promised forever and disappeared.
Maybe you became someone you barely recognized just to keep another person interested.
Maybe you have regrets you cannot undo.
Maybe you are reading this while secretly involved with someone you know is pulling your heart farther from Christ.
Come into the light.
Repent.
Not tomorrow.
Not after one final conversation.
Not after one final night.
Jesus did not shed His blood so you could decorate your chains with Christian vocabulary.
He came to save.
And grace does not merely forgive the person you were.
Grace begins transforming the person you are becoming.
You are not required to drag yesterday's scandal into tomorrow as your identity.
At the cross, guilty people meet a Savior whose mercy is stronger than their worst chapter.
This is why we keep returning to these words:
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
Not by pretending the scandal never happened.
Not by calling sin righteousness.
Not by giving everybody the romantic ending they requested.
He rewrites everything by redeeming sinners.
By forgiving.
By cleansing.
By restoring.
By becoming the center again.
Maybe God will bring someone into your life.
Maybe one day you will look across a room and realize that an ordinary conversation became the beginning of something extraordinary.
Maybe there will be vows.
Maybe there will be children.
Maybe there will be decades together.
If God gives you that gift, receive it with gratitude.
But do not worship it.
And do not build your theology around the assumption that God owes it to you.
Scripture gives Christians hope in Christ; it does not give every believer an individual guarantee of marriage.
That distinction matters.
Because false promises create unnecessary spiritual wreckage.
“Just wait—God has someone for you” sounds comforting.
But unless God has specifically revealed something, we should not promise what Scripture does not promise.
What we can promise is infinitely stronger.
Christ is enough to obey today.
Christ will not become less glorious if your timeline changes.
Christ will not cease being Lord because somebody left.
Christ's cross will not become less sufficient because you are sleeping alone tonight.
Christ's resurrection does not depend upon your relationship status.
And if you belong to Him, your future is ultimately not moving toward a wedding altar on earth.
It is moving toward Christ.
So dream.
Hope.
Pray for marriage if that desire is in you.
Meet people.
Seek wise counsel.
Become emotionally mature.
Learn how to communicate.
Heal where you need healing.
Reject pornography.
Practice sexual holiness.
Develop friendships.
Serve your church.
Build a meaningful life.
Learn generosity.
Become someone capable of covenant faithfulness.
But please...
do not wait to become alive.
You are alive now.
There are people you can love now.
There are lonely people you can notice now.
There are prayers you can pray now.
There is Scripture you can learn now.
There are wounds Christ can address now.
There is holiness to pursue now.
There is Gospel work to do now.
There are people walking toward eternity who need to hear about Jesus now.
Do not sacrifice the life God actually gave you on the altar of the life you imagined He would give you.
And maybe that is the sentence you needed tonight.
Not “stop wanting marriage.”
Not “someone will definitely come.”
But:
Stop making your future wait for a human being before you give it completely to Jesus.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, be honest.
And if Christ has already carried you through heartbreak, comment your testimony. Somebody scrolling through those comments may need proof that heartbreak did not get the final word.
God is glorified by faith, obedience, generosity, love, and lives surrendered to Christ.

Invite your family. Invite the friend who is struggling. Invite the believer who feels spiritually cold. Invite the seeker with difficult questions. Even invite the unbeliever who is willing to listen.
Come back to Jesus.
If romance has become your god, repent.
If rejection became your identity, bring it to Christ.
If loneliness made you compromise, come into the light.
If shame tells you that you are too dirty to return, look again at the cross.
If your imagined future has become more precious than the One who holds your future, open your hands.
You may still desire the wedding.
You may still pray for the person.
You may still cry when the room gets quiet.
Faith does not require pretending.
It requires knowing where to bring the ache.
Bring it to Jesus.
Because one day, whether your earthly story contains the romance you imagined or takes a road you never expected, the deepest question will never have been:
Did somebody finally choose me?
The deepest question is:
Did I belong to Christ?
And if you are His, then your life is not an unfinished love story desperately waiting for another human character to arrive.
Your story already has a center.
His name is Jesus.
Never let the absence of a human hand make you forget the nail-scarred hands that already reached for you.
